advances: An actual all-candidate cover certifies strict improvement from simultaneous cuts even though every small one-point trim strictly worsens the depth. The initial body has depth above the sharper Oertel constant.

proof:
Each binary layer consists of three identical box fibers. Its own mark $(0,\eta,0)$ has raw depth at least $q$ within that layer by symmetry. The two opposite continuous median caps in that layer each have mass $q$ and together cover its planes. To make either an actual ambient cap excluding all other binary layers, add a large positive multiple of $\sum_i(2\eta_i-1)(k_i-\eta_i)$ to its margin. This affine expression is zero on the chosen layer and at most $-1$ on each other layer, and continuous heights are bounded. Thus the total old maximum is exactly $q/(2qL)$. At either noncentral $z$ within a layer an additional sufficiently large finite tilt isolates its own fiber, yielding depth at most $w/2$ there. The ordinary depth of $J$ is $1/2$ by symmetry and opposite median caps. For paired depth, take the average mass of the two parallel tails at equal opposite shifts from a given mark, with infimum over unit continuous normals and shifts before maximizing over marks. At zero the two normalized tails sum to one by continuous reflection symmetry, while zero shift bounds the paired maximum by the ordinary one. The inequality $\Gamma_d<1/2$ follows from $(1+1/d)^d>2$ for $d\ge2$. Every old fiber weighs $w<q=M/2^n$.

An exposed point is a product vertex, and the exposing functional has a strict support gap on the other fibers. Thus every sufficiently small single-point trim changes just one layer. Some other layer remains and its center still has raw depth at least $q$ by its mass contribution alone. The original layer-isolating median caps still cover all candidates, with raw masses at most $q$ since the measure shrinks. This proves the exact single-trim depth.

For the cube, in each layer use the vertex $v_\eta=(1,\eta,1,\ldots,1)$ exposed by $\ell_\eta(z,k,x)=z+\sum_i(2\eta_i-1)k_i+\sum_jx_j$. Its support value is $1+\sum_i\eta_i+d$. A threshold reduction of $t$ removes a simplex given by $\sum_j(1-x_j)<t$ in just the fiber $(1,\eta)$, since each other integer site has support gap at least one. Its volume is $\delta=t^d/d!$. All trims are simultaneous intersections and the old fiber bases remain occupied. At each deepest base the original caps with continuous normals $(1,0,\ldots)$, $(0,1,0,\ldots)$ and $(-1,-1,0,\ldots)/\sqrt2$, with sufficiently large binary-layer tilts as above, have equal mass $q$ and balance with weights $1,1,\sqrt2$. Their section areas in the layer are $q,q,\sqrt2q$, and all other layers are strictly excluded. The normalized reciprocal-section weights are $1/3$ each. The selected vertex in that layer lies in the first two caps and outside the third, and every other selected vertex is excluded. This gives the stated matrix, whose minimum row payoff is $(2/3)\min_\eta\lambda_\eta$. It is maximized by the uniform strategy and is zero when any vertex is omitted.

For a finite exact certificate use, in every layer, the three closed caps with continuous traces $x_1\ge-\delta/(3q)$, $x_2\ge-\delta/(3q)$, and $x_1+x_2\le-2\delta/(3q)$, again extended by isolating tilts. Their continuous traces cover the entire plane and hence each fiber. The removed simplex lies entirely in the first two caps and outside the third. In an old layer either coordinate cut gains $\delta/3$ over the old mass $q$ by constant section area, so after deletion the first two masses are $q-2\delta/3$. The third cap intersects the old square in a triangle of area $(2-h)^2/2$ at level $-h$, with $h=2\delta/(3q)\in[0,2]$. Multiplying by $3\cdot2^{d-2}$ gives $q-qh+qh^2/4=q-2\delta/3+\delta^2/(9q)$, unchanged by deletion. Divide this largest covering mass by $L(2q-\delta)$ and simplify. The strict inequality and the nonheavy condition follow from $\delta<w$ and $M_{\rm new}/2^n=(3w-\delta)/2>w$.

statement:
Fix $n,d\ge2$, $L=2^{n-1}$ and a full-dimensional rectangular box $J\subset\mathbb R^d$ centered at zero, with volume $w$. Use the actual integer fibers of
$$
C=[-1,1]\times[0,1]^{n-1}\times J.
$$
Writing $q=3w/2$, the normalized maximum closed-halfspace depth is $\beta=1/(2L)=2^{-n}$, its deepest bases are the $(0,\eta)$ with $\eta\in\{0,1\}^{n-1}$, and every fiber has mass $w<M/2^n$. The ordinary and paired maximum depths of $J$ are both $1/2>\Gamma_d$. For each fixed supporting plane exposing a single point of $C$, every sufficiently small inward translation of that plane, removing mixed mass $\varepsilon>0$, gives exact new maximum $q/(2qL-\varepsilon)>\beta$.

For the cube $J=[-1,1]^d$, there is a simultaneous family of $L$ vertex trims, one in each binary layer, each removing $\delta=t^d/d!$ for $0<t\le1$, whose actual full normalized depth satisfies
$$
D_{\rm new}\le\frac{q-2\delta/3+\delta^2/(9q)}{L(2q-\delta)}
=\frac1{2L}-\frac{\delta(3q-2\delta)}{18qL(2q-\delta)}
<\frac1{2L}.
$$
The new source also has no heavy fiber. The selected equal-slope incidence game for these $L$ vertices and $L$ deepest bases has matrix $(2/3)I_L$, value $2/(3L)$, and every profitable strategy uses all $L$ vertices.
title: Protected box layers admit simultaneous descent despite every single-point trim increasing depth
